articles.title: Hegseth puts Musk, Luckey, Gingrich in charge of military future warfare review
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday announced that SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk, Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.) will lead a new Pentagon effort to study the future of warfare, dubbed “Project Meridian.” The Pentagon chief said the project is meant to harness America’s innovators, senior leaders and technologists to look…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday announced that SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk, Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.) will lead a new Pentagon effort to study the future of warfare, dubbed “Project Meridian.”

The Pentagon chief said the project is meant to harness America’s innovators, senior leaders and technologists to look decades into the future and “forecast the creative solution for tomorrow’s conflicts.”

“It is futuristic on purpose,” he said of the project, noting it was not meant to develop new strategies or policies.

“We should have the humility to recognize that the best forecasters of future conflict do not solely reside inside the Pentagon,” Hegseth continued. “There are obvious biases and risks to asking ourselves to both ask the questions and answer them.”

Hegseth said Musk, Luckey and Gingrich — under the leadership of Emil Michael, undersecretary of Defense for research and engineering — “will be focused on discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes, without any creative limitations or restrictions, on any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon.”

All three men were in attendance at the Pentagon as Hegseth made his announcement, and the Pentagon chief said their first meeting on Project Meridian would happen directly after the event in a sensitive, compartmented information facility in the building.

“Right after this speech, we are going to hit the ground running, and in that time, Project Meridian will ruthlessly map the trajectory of wars, domains and technologies to ensure this War Department, your War Department, dominates the future,” Hegseth said.

A memo released shortly after the announcement stressed that the U.S. military “must not take our current advantages for granted” as the world witnesses rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology and other high-tech areas.

“Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare,” according to the Sept. 30 memo. “To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them.”

Hegseth directed Michael to commission Project Meridian to “study the battlefields of the future, identify which weapons and technologies warfighters will need to harness to dominate in these environments, and propose actionable solutions to start developing, testing and fielding these capabilities” no later than Jan. 28, or 120 days from now.

Project Meridian also will call on “a group of top technologists, innovators, business leaders, policy makers, and national security experts” to come up with proposed solutions.

He adds that the Joint Staff and all services should be prepared to connect their future warfare efforts and research to Project Meridian.

articles.summary: Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) blocked an effort from Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) on Wednesday to pass by unanimous consent the Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA), a long-sought bill that intends to protect kids in the digital space. articles.body:
Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) blocked an effort from Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) on Wednesday to pass by unanimous consent the Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA), a long-sought bill that intends to protect kids in the digital space.

KOSA, which aims to hold accountable social media companies for the alleged harms their platforms cause for young children and teens, has long had support from the majority of senators, but differences with the House stopped it from passing both chambers in 2024.

Unlike the House version that passed as part of a broader package last summer, the Senate’s KOSA includes a “duty of care” provision, which would legally require platforms to “exercise reasonable care” to prevent harms to minors. Harms include eating disorders, suicide, substance use disorders and sexual exploitation.

The duty of care provision is a red line for KOSA co-authors Blackburn and Blumenthal, along with several tech watchdogs that have pushed for KOSA to pass for years.

The Senate version passed out of committee last month, and the legislative calendar is running out this year to come to an agreement with the House.

Lawmakers introduced KOSA four times in as many years, and while it passed the Senate easily in 2024, House Republicans’ concerns over censorship and freedom of speech prevented it from ever hitting the House floor.

articles.body:
South Korea’s government will invest up to $200 billion in U.S. energy infrastructure, including a natural gas pipeline in Alaska, President Trump announced Wednesday.

The investment also includes a natural gas plant in Texas and eight new nuclear power plants across the country, Trump said during remarks in the Oval Office.

Trump said the deal came as part of a trade agreement between South Korea and the U.S. in which the U.S. would lower the Asian country’s tariff rate to 15 percent in exchange for hundreds of billions of dollars in investment.

Trump particularly touted the Alaska pipeline investment, known as Alaska LNG because it would transport liquefied natural gas, as allowing the U.S. to export more gas.

“The United States is already the largest natural gas producer and exporter in the world, and this pipeline will help us expand those exports even further,” he said.

Alaska LNG, an 807-mile vessel, is expected to receive a $54 billion investment from Korea. In the Oval Office, Trump touted the involvement of Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), who is running to retain his seat against several candidates, including former Rep. Mary Peltola (D).

The White House described the Alaska LNG project as the largest proposed energy infrastructure project in U.S. history.

articles.title: Pennsylvania records 5th measles-related death this year
articles.summary: Pennsylvania health officials reported a fifth measles-associated death Wednesday amid a rapidly growing outbreak — the worst outbreak the commonwealth has seen in more than 35 years. The Pennsylvania Department of Health said the person who died was unvaccinated and a resident of Lancaster County, but it did not release more information. Officials in a statement…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania health officials reported a fifth measles-associated death Wednesday amid a rapidly growing outbreak — the worst outbreak the commonwealth has seen in more than 35 years.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health said the person who died was unvaccinated and a resident of Lancaster County, but it did not release more information.

Officials in a statement said the death “meets the measles-associated death definition” and has been reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

There are now 943 measles cases in Pennsylvania, with about 40 percent concentrated in Lancaster County. According to official state figures, there have been at least 176 hospitalizations. All but four of the cases have been among people who were not fully vaccinated.

The other deaths include an unvaccinated 18-year-old in Mifflin County, a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County and two infants in Lancaster County.

But the CDC has refused to acknowledge the same number of deaths as the Keystone State, sparking a bitter political dispute between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) — a potential 2028 presidential candidate — and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over what constitutes a measles death.

The agency to date has only recognized two deaths. The CDC’s database also does not specify where or when these deaths occurred, so it’s not clear if the tally includes Pennsylvania’s reported cases. However, no other state has recorded a measles death this year.

Pennsylvania is currently reporting the highest total number of measles cases in the U.S.

Earlier this month, Pennsylvania’s health department started the process of requesting emergency assistance from the CDC’s Epi-Aid program, but only on the condition that the CDC publicly recognize the state’s death count.

According to spokesperson for the Pennsylvania Department of Health, there are ongoing discussions and meetings between CDC staff and Pennsylvania officials about a potential focus for the Epi-Aid, but nothing has been finalized.

There are at least 3,659 measles cases in the U.S., according to the CDC. The last time there were more than four measles deaths in a year was 1991.

Last year, three people in the U.S. died from measles — two in Texas and one in New Mexico.

articles.title: Hegseth announces 5 new non-Ivy League partnerships
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced new Pentagon partnerships with five non-Ivy League colleges and universities Wednesday amid his ongoing efforts to distance the military from America’s most prestigious higher education institutions. “We’re partnering with a new crop of premier higher ed institutions, including Louisiana State University [LSU], Liberty University, Tuskegee University, Mississippi State University and…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced new Pentagon partnerships with five non-Ivy League colleges and universities Wednesday amid his ongoing efforts to distance the military from America’s most prestigious higher education institutions.

“We’re partnering with a new crop of premier higher ed institutions, including Louisiana State University [LSU], Liberty University, Tuskegee University, Mississippi State University and Hillsdale College,” Hegseth said during a speech Wednesday in Quantico, Va.

“These schools have stepped forward to answer the call to duty and establish new corps of cadets in partnership with the Department of War,” Hegseth added, using his preferred term for the Department of Defense. “So today, at my direction, we are formally establishing a program to assist these universities and colleges. It’s called, ‘America’s Corps of Cadets.’”

The announcement came months after he ordered the cancellation of members of the military attending some Ivy League and top-ranked universities, alleging in February that the schools taught the “enemy’s wicked ideologies.”

Hegseth said during his speech that the new program “is central to our goal of increasing the number of patriotic leaders of character who are commissioned into our joint force.”

Earlier this year, Hegseth restricted military officers from taking part in graduate programs at multiple elite universities, including Harvard University, Brown University, Princeton University and Yale University.

The Defense secretary, an alumnus of Harvard and Princeton, claimed these schools had turned into “woke breeding grounds of toxic indoctrination.”

Two months ago, the Defense Department chose the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and Virginia Tech to host a refurbished fellowship program for senior military officers. Both schools were selected for the new Senior Service College Fellowship, a professional military education program lasting 10 months and serving as an alternative to traditional war colleges.

Schools in “America’s Corps of Cadets” “will maintain exceptionally high standards of cadet discipline, tactical instruction and military organization,” Hegseth said. He added the five higher education institutions will receive “Honor School” status, which he said will grant them “priority in officer commissioning.”

Hegseth said the Pentagon previously used the “distinguished military college” label and is bringing it back for the new program. Its implementation will commence within the month, according to an announcement memo .

articles.title: 7 takeaways from Hegseth’s address to officers: Warfare’s future, faith and a new base
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a flurry of announcements during a wide-ranging speech to active-duty officers Wednesday. At the beginning of the address, the Pentagon chief stuck to his bread and butter: culture-war grievances, stripping the “woke” out of the Department of Defense (DOD), bashing the news media for its coverage of the Iran war,…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a flurry of announcements during a wide-ranging speech to active-duty officers Wednesday.

At the beginning of the address, the Pentagon chief stuck to his bread and butter: culture-war grievances , stripping the “woke” out of the Department of Defense (DOD), bashing the news media for its coverage of the Iran war, and proclaiming the “warrior ethos” has been revived and the U.S. military has been “rebuilt.”

But the Defense secretary made several newsy announcements that lean into Hegseth’s elevation of faith, create a combatant command, partner the Pentagon with different universities and tease a new domestic military base for which governors will compete.

Here are the takeaways from Hegseth’s 52-minute speech at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia:

New combatant command focused on autonomous warfare

Hegseth announced the formation of a new four-star combatant command focused on developing autonomous warfare like drones and defense robotics.

The Defense secretary said it would have “service-like authorities built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force in the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history,” with the aim of being operational by Oct. 1 next year.

The Autonomous Warfare Command, or “AutoWarCom,” will be initially led by Owen West, a former Marine who is now the director of the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit, and Max Strasiser, a Navy SEAL senior chief. Later, a four-star military leader will be announced.

“This command will possess directed manpower, budget, acquisition authorities and create dedicated military career pathways for Officers and Enlisted personnel,” Hegseth said in a Wednesday memo .

The new command will test equipment and force designs with “realistic opposition” in exercises and rugged environments to figure out what works on the battlefield, the Defense secretary said in the memo.

Hegseth revealed that SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk, Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.) will lead a new Pentagon effort to study the future of warfare, dubbed Project Meridian.

The Pentagon chief said the project is meant to harness America’s innovators, senior leaders and technologists to look decades into the future and “forecast the creative solution for tomorrow’s conflicts.”

“It is futuristic on purpose,” he said of the project, which he clarified was not meant to develop new strategies or policies.

“We should have the humility to recognize that the best forecasters of future conflict do not solely reside inside the Pentagon,” Hegseth said. “There are obvious biases and risks to asking ourselves to both ask the questions and answer them.”

Hegseth said Musk, Luckey and Gingrich, under the leadership of Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, “will be focused on discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes, without any creative limitations or restrictions, on any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon.”

All three men were in attendance at the Pentagon as Hegseth made his announcement, and the Pentagon chief said their first meeting on Project Meridian would happen immediately following the event in a sensitive compartmented information facility in the building.

States invited to bid for ‘next great American’ base

Hegseth invited governors to bid for their state to be the home of the “next great American” base.

“We’re calling on every governor in the country and adjutant general, every tag across this great republic, to step up to the plate and bring us their best sales pitch,” the Defense secretary said.

“If your state wants the honor of hosting 15,000 to 25,000 of America’s great troops, show us why and how you’re going to do it, cutting through the red tape, offering up the land and rolling out the red carpet for our military families,” he said during the speech.

Naval Station Everett in Washington state was the most recent base built inside the U.S., opening in the 1990s. The base is home to several guided-missile destroyers and Coast Guard ships.

Hegseth said the new base will not be a “soulless government installation,” arguing the Pentagon will “plan out and chart out a dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform.”

The Pentagon said the base will be off the commercial grid, featuring independent power generation, autonomous systems and advanced air defenses.

“We’re talking hundreds of thousands of acres with organic power generation, modern air defenses, and cutting-edge technology, think a fortress,” the secretary said. Service members will have “first-class barracks, world-class training facilities, and thriving communities with top-tier housing, school, childcare and healthcare for families.”

Hegseth directed Dale R. Marks, who is assistant secretary of Defense for energy, installations and environment, to lead the Pentagon’s effort to identify, evaluate, select and prepare an optimal site for the base.

“Rapid advancements in disruptive technologies, growing strategic alignment among peer adversaries, and persistent, sophisticated cyber intrusions against critical defense and homeland infrastructure necessitate a modernized, resilient posture,” the Defense secretary said in a Wednesday memo.

‘Fortress America’ takes bases off civilian grid

Another new initiative revealed Wednesday is “Fortress America,” which Hegseth claimed will be “a national insurance policy for the American homeland.”

Under Fortress, which stands for “Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy Supply and Survivability,” every major military installation in America would generate its own power independent of the civilian grid, according to Hegseth.

“If an adversary takes down the grid by cyberattack, by sabotage, or by any means, our bases stay lit. Our aircraft keep flying. Our command centers never go dark,” he said.

The effort also is meant to bring critical supply chains home, including rare earth minerals, specialty metals, semiconductors and propellants “mined in America, refined in America, built in America by American workers.”

In addition, the Pentagon would build up strategic reserves of such critical needs as munitions, fuel, medicine and blood “deep enough that if the world’s supply lines break — and in a real war, they’re going to break — America keeps fighting anyway,” Hegseth said.

To accomplish this, Hegseth said the U.S. military is “hardening every installation on American soil against cyber intrusion, sabotage and drones, and we’re securing the high ground and the airwaves, our satellites, our spectrum,” claiming that the DOD “will be the insurance policy for the entire nation.”

New non-Ivy League partnerships for cadets

The Defense secretary also said the Pentagon will partner with five more colleges to broaden the corps of cadets.

The military training program, called “America’s Corps of Cadets,” will include Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Tuskegee University, Mississippi State University and Hillsdale College.

“We need more officers from academic institutions like our military academies and senior military colleges, and today we’re going to make that happen,” Hegseth said.

Each school will be a “distinguished military college” and will be expected to “maintain exceptionally high standards of cadet discipline, tactical instruction and military organization,” the Pentagon chief said.

Military academies like West Point, Naval Academy and Air Force Academy commission most of the officers into the U.S. armed forces, followed by senior military colleges like Texas A&M and the Citadel.

Hegseth’s office will begin implementation within 30 days, and within four months, Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata will transition to become the primary office responsible for the program, according to a Wednesday Pentagon memo .

“From the Ivy Leagues to the most liberal arts colleges, our colleges and universities have become anti-American DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion] worshipping woke factories. Qualities like grit and courage replaced with political correctness and social justice,” Hegseth said. “God and country traded for Che Guevara and critical theory.”

In his last proclamation, Hegseth declared he will establish the Office of Religious Affairs at the Pentagon that “will report straight to the top.”

“Cutting-edge technology … new basing and bases … and a better educational pipeline are still incomplete without the most essential component of our republic: faith,” he told the assembled service members.

He said the Defense Department has “a sacred duty” to provide troops with “first-class religious support” wherever they’re sent, bashing past administrations for treating the topic as an afterthought.

“Political correctness and secular humanism got a vote. Chaplains did not. Budgets were cut. Resourcing and manpower needs were ignored. Base chapels fell apart,” Hegseth claimed. “Decisions about faith and religion were made by secular careerists in cubicles and lawyers running around with red tape.”

Starting Wednesday, the Office of Religious Affairs will have “a direct line to the secretary” and will “protect budgets, demand infrastructure, and strengthen religious support,” he said.

Hegseth frequently invokes his faith and has declared service members’ spiritual health as “equally important” as their physical and mental health.

Earlier this year he revamped the U.S. military’s Chaplain Corps, announcing that the officers will no longer wear their rank insignia, instead displaying insignia that reflects their religious affiliation — part of two major changes to the group.

At the start of his speech, Hegseth defended his plan to cut 20 percent of generals and admirals at the Pentagon, arguing the major shake-up was long overdue at the department.

“Now the media calls that a purge. I call it accountability and long overdue, and frankly, the bare minimum. As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment,” Hegseth said.

“You see, you can’t change a culture with the same people who enabled it,” he said. “Personnel is policy at every single level.”

The move will impact senior leadership positions across the Army, Navy and the Air Force, coming a year after Hegseth oversaw a 10 percent reduction of general officers.

The move comes as he has already fired or pushed out more than two dozen senior military officers across the service branches, personnel changes that have unnerved congressional lawmakers on both sides of the aisle .

“You see, last year’s speech was not for those generals,” Hegseth said during the speech. “It was for you, the backbone of our force, the current and future leaders on the front lines.”

The 6 new initiatives in Hegseth’s Pentagon

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday gave a wide-ranging speech to active-duty officers at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Va., unveiling six new efforts .

The 52-min speech included the announcement of a new combatant command focused on developing autonomous warfare, the Pentagon’s new partnerships with colleges, a new Office of Religious Affairs and inviting governors to help build a new military base inside the country.

But the event was not without Hegseth’s well-trodden comments on culture-war grievances , stripping the “ woke ” out of the Pentagon, lambasting the news media for its coverage of the Iran war and proclamations that the “warrior ethos” has been revived and the U.S. military has been “rebuilt.”

“I like to think last year’s Quantico speech was ‘Liberation Day’ for leaders, for you, to be the apolitical, hard-charging, commonsense, no-nonsense constitutional leaders that you joined the military to be,” Hegseth said, referring to his address last September to nearly all of the U.S. military’s generals and admirals.

“We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: No fatties, no t——-, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors ,” Hegseth continued, using a pejorative term for transgender individuals.

Also at the top of the speech, Hegseth defended his plan to cut 20 percent of generals and admirals at the Pentagon, arguing the major shake-up was “long overdue” at the department.

My colleague Filip Timotija and I watched the speech and have a full breakdown of the six new initiatives announced and who will lead the efforts.

Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & National Security newsletter, I’m Ellen Mitchell — your guide to the latest developments at the Pentagon, on Capitol Hill and beyond.

articles.title: Android Central, a good blog, has been gutted.
articles.summary:
Staffers don’t know whether the site will shut down — but managing editor Derrek Lee confirms to The Verge that all remaining staff were laid off today. EIC Shruti Shekar confirms she’s been laid off, senior editor Harish Jonnalagadda and senior content producer Nicolas Sutrich wrote they’d been laid off, and senior editor Namarah Saud Fatmi also appears to be gone.
Android Central’s masthead was already down to six staffers after layoffs earlier this year. Earlier today, owner Future PLC announced it would pause its share buyback and focus on reducing debt.

articles.body:
A man was arrested after making “verbal threats” toward the Texas State Capitol, the Lone Star State’s governor, Greg Abbott (R), confirmed Wednesday evening.

On Wednesday, the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) told NBC Dallas-Fort Worth that authorities had stopped a plot on the state’s capitol building in Austin. Per the outlet, DPS said law enforcement had obtained a credible threat of an attack planned for Thursday.

The department arrested Benny Caldera Jr., 40, in the San Antonio area early Wednesday morning in connection with the incident. DPS said it had collaborated with the FBI before the arrest to investigate the threat’s credibility.

Caldera’s friend, per an arrest warrant affidavit, had told DPS officers that the man “had made verbal threats to assault the Texas State Capitol Building,” NBC reported.

In a post on the social platform X, Abbott wrote, “Texas DPS and the FBI stopped a planned attack on the Texas Capitol.”

“Texas will NOT tolerate threats of violence against our Capitol,” he added, before thanking DPS for its response.

According to arrest documents obtained by NBC, Caldera reportedly told his friend he had anger toward the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), allegedly adding, “These people have to be exterminated.”

articles.body:
Indiana Gov. Mike Braun (R) said Wednesday he is extending his state’s gas tax suspension as fuel prices elevate due to the ongoing war in Iran

“Today I announced another gas tax extension with additional relief for farmers,” Braun said in a post to social platform X. “Our farmers have the hardest job in America.”

“The added cost of fuel prices caused by continued disruptions to the global oil supply can make a major difference in our farmers’ success and their ability to put food on the table for their families,” the governor added.

Braun said the tax suspension would go “through early November.”

Lawmakers and candidates in other Midwest states , including Iowa and Ohio, have pushed for a rapid end to the war in Iran amid high fuel prices and the conflict’s increasing unpopularity. The conflict has resulted in multiple Republicans dealing with challenging reelection campaigns.

In early April, Braun halted his state’s sales tax on gas for 30 days and has extended it several times since.

“The state will be watching the pumps to make sure savings are delivered to Hoosiers when they go to fill up each week, or whenever they do,” the governor said at the time.

Global energy costs have risen since the U.S. and Israel launched their attack against Iran in late February, leading to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a key waterway for the oil industry.

As of Wednesday night, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was about $4.43, up from about $3.15 last year at the same time, according to AAA. At the same time, the average price of a gallon of gas in Indiana was about $3.83 — up from $3.09 in September 2025.
